title: The Firefly Cage
summary: First dance in Lavenham. Lovejoy gets dragged into murder and theft before anyone explains what a divvy is. Ends with a boozy mop fight on a boat.
divvyMoment: Sees a Napoleonic sea fort in the silhouette of a firefly cage
guestStar: Kim Thomson, Ronald Fraser & Sarah Lawson
body: One Wink Plot Avengers assemble; then a client asks Lovejoy to authenticate a Japanese firefly cage. By the end of the episode there has been a theft, a murder, a treasure hunt and a whisky-fuelled boat chase. Review "Who will start me for a hundred? Don't lose it for another fifty. Lovejoy!" And we are off. Episode 1, Series 1. Watching this now — over 40 years later — and I would still be hooked. What a start. The plan is to review an episode every week until we reach The Last Tango in Lavenham in 18 months or so. Why (I don't hear anyone say)? Well, over the (many) years I've kept coming back to Lovejoy. And as my ability to focus on anything for longer than a few minutes starts to become a cause for a murmur of concern, what better way to bring some disciplined focus back than to actually watch (no phone) some Lovejoy episodes and then comment on them. Dilapidated Volvo, Huey Lewis and the News, Power of Love floating over the Suffolk countryside. Lovejoy emerges from a smoking Volvo estate (a modern-day antique car) into a bucolic Constable-esque scene — a slightly dishevelled thatched cottage at the end of a farm lane, fields, hazy sunlight. Cut to Eric in a market town square, listening to hair metal on a quaint old tape/walkman type thing. Plays cassette tapes — Eric looks like a C90 man to these experienced eyes. Turns out his butcher dad is prepared to pay this Lovejoy to train hapless drifting vegan Eric in the way of the divvy. Gimbert is delivered up next — cigar in mouth and sly smile. We have our villain and Lovejoy's nemesis slash landlord. Not quite Joffrey Baratheon; more a Tom to Lovejoy's Jerry. It is implied later that Jerry has deflowered Tom's sister. Not sure Looney Tunes covered this. "If home is where the heart is, then this is home to me," says Lovejoy to the camera in the antiques auction house. The fourth wall collapses as quickly as Spurs' midfield. And next — ah, tits — now we have Dandy Jack. Three big hitters and then a distinctly softer fourth. The name suggests a crazy bon vivant. Instead, we get a posh bank manager type who appears half-heartedly in a lot of series 1 episodes and then, after the five-year hiatus between series 1 and 2, is dropped (although in the fantastic Bin Diving episode in S2E3 we do get a call to Dandy from Lovejoy for continuity's sake). Lovejoy's universe answer to Jar Jar Binks. Dandy will be back. Offering Jack. Tinker up next. One of the big five. Only minutes in, and the main cast are mainly with us, and they seem fully formed already. Tinker explains what a barker is to Eric (lesson number one; the lessons dry up after this tidbit — I was going to measure, but nowt's worth measuring) and that he is one (an alcoholic who sniffs out antiques, which seems to be the general gist). Now we have settled on our holy triumvirate: Lovejoy, Tinker, and Eric. A divvy, a barker, and a City & Guilds student. Spot. On. Lot 29. What turns out to be the Bamboo Japanese Firefly Cage. The other bidders are throwing their arms around like they're signalling for a plane to land. Not Lovejoy. Just the most subtle of left (always left) half-closed eye winks, and his bid is accepted. Unfortunately, the police arrive mid-bidding to arrest Lovejoy — and no one seems surprised. A loveable rogue. The lady who was bidding against Lovejoy wins. The mysterious bamboo lady turns out not to be Lysette Anthony, despite my memory insisting otherwise. This is Kim Thomson. Lysette will arrive later to continue Lovejoy's long-running commitment to age-gap diplomacy and proving he isn't yet 'Deadwood'. At the police station, Lovejoy explains that although he deals in stolen-looking antiques, he doesn't actually steal them. This defence works surprisingly well. The Suffolk constabulary would no doubt have accepted it with the same alacrity as Prince Andrew's lack of sweat and fondness for Pizza Hut. Still only 10 minutes in, and the script, the acting, the scenery are as masterfully curated as a Fabergé egg. Within minutes of meeting Eric, Lovejoy has commandeered both the man/apprentice and his sidecar. Recruitment standards in mid-80s Suffolk were refreshingly low. No LinkedIn profile needed. Our own Wallace and Gromit then splash Lady Jane, who is hanging around by the said forge. The water obstacle appears to punch a hole in the space-time continuum. Moments later it is dark, Eric is pushing the bike, and they have stumbled across a burglary in a house Lovejoy knows should be empty. Anyway (and a heads up going forward, most reviews won't be this detailed, more sort of emotion/general feeling — but the first episode is a pure delight and it is... the first episode!), we are now in Lovejoy's barn cum workshop, and this place looks great. Bric-a-brac all over the place. Tea cups, paper. It is what I think of when I think of Lovejoy. Lovejoy will move out after series 1, although the cynic in me suspects the replacement barn was built by the same set designer with access to the same pile of junk. The episode then descends into a treasure hunt involving a carved lump of coal, several dead people, a JCB dealer, and what I assume was a perfectly coherent chain of logic in somebody's head. It ends (I kid you not) with a boat chase and Tinker giving up his remaining whisky to douse a mop so Lovejoy can launch it aflame at the other boat. I've watched this three times recently and still understand it only slightly better than Ulysses. But it doesn't matter. None of it should quite work, and yet it does. Upon watching this again after so many years, I was worried it wouldn't stand up. It does. If home is where the heart is, then a settee and an episode of Lovejoy is home to me.

title: The Axeman Cometh
summary: Post-pilot shenanigans. Lovejoy buys a battered Welsh oak dresser and discovers a hidden compartment stuffed with treasure and several cultural assumptions that wouldn't survive a modern People Team presentation.
body: One Wink Plot One antique dresser, one secret drawer and one recently released psychopath. What could possibly go wrong? Also, somehow, we're back on a boat for a budget East Anglian remake of Captain Phillips. Review "You'd better run, you'd better hide..." "Here come the twentieth century's latest scam..." This episode starts brilliantly. Nick Lowe's Half a Boy and Half a Man drifts through the opening sequence while Lovejoy tunelessly sings along, and for twenty minutes or so The Axeman Cometh feels like the show settling into the formula that would carry it through the next six series. Unfortunately, once the action moves to London it loses a little momentum and wanders into the kind of ethnic stereotyping that hasn't been fashionable since Alf Garnett was considered cutting-edge entertainment. After spotting a magnificent Welsh oak dresser at auction, Lovejoy employs one of his trademark manoeuvres to keep it out of rival Charlie Gimbert's hands. The resulting auction scene gives us the immortal cry heard in the opening titles: "At three fifty. Lovejoy!" So now we know. It was the dresser all along. The opening scenes are a delight. First, a frantic car chase through Suffolk lanes as Lovejoy attempts to evade what appears to be a criminal mastermind but turns out to be something far more terrifying: a tax collector. Then it's off through the market square, into Dandy Jack's antiques shop to hide out (which, in fairness, is pretty much Dandy's entire contribution to the episode), and finally into the café where the tax lady catches up with him. Lovejoy owes £10,000. The dresser itself contains a hidden compartment concealing an Arabian bridal headdress decorated with Venetian gold ducats. Lovejoy immediately places it on Lady Jane's head and both admire it reverentially. To my eyes it resembles a cross between a medieval mail coif and something issued by the NHS for a particularly unfortunate course of chemotherapy. Consulting Friedberg's Gold Coins of the World (which, remarkably, turns out to be a real book), Lovejoy calculates that the twelve Venetian ducats are worth around $27,000. Why the valuation is in dollars rather than pounds remains one of the episode's lesser mysteries. Naturally, such treasures cannot possibly be sold in Lavenham, so off to London our hero trots. Unfortunately this is where the episode loses some of its charm. The Fantastic Four of Lovejoy, Lady Jane, Eric and Gimbert are largely left behind in favour of a collection of less memorable London characters. Chief among them are Vial, a French dealer whom Lovejoy barely seemed to know at the auction but now treats like an old friend, and an eccentric Jewish coin expert whose characterisation feels rather more 1936 than 1986. Meanwhile, newly released psychopath Catesby is on the trail. Having spent years in prison dreaming of the treasure hidden inside his Welsh dresser, he is understandably annoyed to discover that while the dresser has been returned, the valuable contents have not. Armed with an axe, a grievance and what may be the most enthusiastic Welsh (hint of Cockney) accent committed to British television, he sets off in pursuit. And because this is apparently a nautical series now, the climax eventually unfolds aboard a London narrowboat in a hostage situation that feels suspiciously like somebody accidentally remade Captain Phillips three decades early and on a considerably tighter budget. "You'd better run, you'd better hide..." Unfortunately, that's exactly what the episode does. As soon as Lovejoy and the plot run down to London, both start to lose their way. Much like Murder, She Wrote, the episodes away from Cabot Cove are rarely as good as the ones set there. Lovejoy belongs in Suffolk market squares, village auctions and slightly shabby antique shops. Remove him from that world and some of the magic disappears.

title: The Sting
summary: Lovejoy is hired by a reformed junkie to recover statuettes she stole from her dying father. Charlie Gimbert double-crosses him at the auction. The gang reassembles for what is essentially Newman-and-Redford on £8.50.
divvyMoment: A wink is as good as a flag to an auctioneer
body: One Wink Plot Lovejoy's first proper caper. A reformed junkie hires him to recover statuettes she pinched from her dying father; Charlie Gimbert double-crosses him at the auction; revenge comes via a long con featuring a forger, a barker, a vegan apprentice, an addict and an aristocrat. Review "I need you, Lovejoy. Since my wife died, I need someone to hate." This is the one. After two episodes finding its feet — the masterful Firefly Cage and the slightly wobbly Welsh dresser — The Sting is where Lovejoy properly clicks. Five out of five. If a friend has somehow staggered into 2026 without ever seeing an episode, this is where I'd start them. The episode opens with a delicious feint: Lovejoy himself behind the rostrum, gavelling down a fifteenth-century Korean vase. Our McMuffin (or McGuffin, if you must), or so we are led to believe. Of course it isn't. It never is. And speaking of period authenticity — Hard Rock Café gets a name-check. A perfect 1986 signifier, except weirdly permanent: queuing for fashionable restaurants is somehow still A Thing in 2026. The bit that doesn't translate is everything else. Pre-internet. Pre-mobile. Ten years before either. You forget how recently we lived in a world where you couldn't just look it up. Reassuringly recognisable, but — blimey — different enough. Our client this week is Corinna Hope: reformed junkie, embezzler, daughter to a dying father whose estate is about to be catalogued by people who will notice a few missing statuettes. Her former drug pusher turns up in act one, looking less like a menace and more like a Knightsbridge estate agent with a slightly-too-good car. Zero threat. Even the menace is posh. The plot is labyrinthine again, but it winds entirely through auction houses — and the BBC was always extraordinary at filming rooms full of polished mahogany and the quiet hum of money changing hands. That alone is reason enough to recommend it. The whole crew is in: Eric on apprentice duty, Tinker tipsy and quotable, Lady Jane elegant and amused, Dandy Jack… still mostly hiding. I include his picture. Then the Gimbert speech, delivered while shooting clay pigeons with the air of a man for whom a Saturday morning is essentially grief management: "I need you, Lovejoy. Since my wife died, I need someone to hate." It is a brilliant line, and an even better delivery from Malcolm Tierney — sour, wounded, completely sincere about the loathing. So sincere that the late Mrs Gimbert is, naturally, never spoken of again. Lovejoy's universe doesn't really do grief. Or continuity. Special mention for Fred, Gimbert's put-upon henchman, who performs his duties with the resigned air of a man whose career options have been narrowed to "this" or "honest work." Some of the funniest lines in the episode are his, mostly delivered from a half-step behind Gimbert and at an angle suggesting he'd rather be in actual prison. Best individual scene in the episode: Lady Jane has rushed back from a friend's wedding, kicks her heels off, and plays pool with Lovejoy in the pub. Forty years on, the chemistry between McShane and Logan still does the work that sixty minutes of plotting cannot. You watch them rack up the balls and you understand exactly why this show worked. The forgery sequence is a genuine joy. A few glugs of red wine, a couple of laps round the oven and a splash of turps, and Tinker's contributions are ready for market. Aged, as the kids would say, like Cliff Richard. And mid-auction, Lovejoy turns to camera with the line that — more than the gavel, the dodgy Volvo or the leather jacket — actually defines what the show is about: "A wink is as good as a flag to an auctioneer." That is the entire premise of the divvy in one tidy sentence. Print it on a T-shirt; I'll buy six. A final, perfect grace note. At the climactic auction the auctioneer takes Lady Jane's winning bid with a polite "Sold to Mrs Felsham." Janey's eyebrow goes up by maybe half a millimetre — but it does go up. There are limits to her proletarianism, as it turns out. Her ladyship will happily slum it with the antiques crowd, but not at the expense of being correctly addressed. All for one, and one for Gimbert. The first time the ensemble pulls a job together, and the show works out what it is. If you've never seen an episode of Lovejoy in your life, watch this one. The rest will follow.

title: Friends, Romans and Enemies
summary: A dead master forger sends half the antiques trade on a treasure hunt for Roman coins, while Lovejoy chases clues across the Isle of Man and is repeatedly distracted by a blonde American. Gimbert shoots at his tenant, Dandy survives an attempted murder and somehow Lovejoy still ends up pocketing a few coins for a rainy day.
divvyMoment: You're like putty when you see a bit of skirt
body: One Wink Plot A dead master forger sends half the antiques trade on a treasure hunt for Roman coins, while Lovejoy chases clues across the Isle of Man and is repeatedly distracted by a blonde American. Gimbert shoots at his tenant, Dandy survives an attempted murder and somehow Lovejoy still ends up pocketing a few coins for a rainy day. Review "You're like putty, you are Lovejoy, when you see a bit of skirt." Quite possibly the most accurate character assessment delivered in the first series so far. Things begin beautifully with a callback to the opening episode and the lane leading to Lovejoy's cottage. This time, however, Gimbert is waiting with a double-barrelled shotgun. Side-by-side barrels too, if my Young Farmers education from the 1980s taught me anything beyond livestock judging and avoiding dubious cider. Incredibly, Gimbert actually fires at his tenant. A lively start. "What do you want, Gimbert?" "My rent." The sort of landlord dispute that would nowadays involve mediation, several forms and perhaps a strongly worded email. In Suffolk, apparently, it involves buckshot. Then comes another wonderful Gimbert revelation. "I despise you. You deflowered my sister." The episode continues expanding the Lovejoy dictionary. We learn about a "scan" — rummaging through vast amounts of junk looking for hidden treasure — and being "on the knock", tramping door-to-door asking after antiques. Lovejoy tells us - the viewer this - not sure if he tells Eric. Being on the knock appears to be the antiques trade equivalent of financial distress. Rather like minesweeping at a wedding buffet for unattended vol-au-vents. Meanwhile Eric offers Lovejoy even more money to continue his education. Good news all round, as I wasn't quite ready to lose Eric to UB40 and Lovejoy to lead poisoning. The mystery centres around Roman coins linked to the late Bexton, master forger, rogue and part-time chaos merchant. Turns out this innocent little "scan" of the Bexton estate has unleashed chaos. Even in death, Bexton is still manipulating dealers, collectors and treasure hunters. Rather than leaving behind money, he's left behind clues. The result is less archaeology and more a nationwide antiques-themed treasure hunt organised by a dead practical joker. We're told the Isle of Man was never conquered by the Romans. Remarkably this is true. Unfortunately it also means we are eventually heading there. Unlike Episode 2 's London excursion, however, Friends, Romans and Enemies survives the journey perfectly well. The secret turns out not to be location but atmosphere. The episode remains firmly rooted in antiques, scams and eccentrics. The first half is particularly glorious. Lovejoy's cottage. The pub and its permanently unimpressed Tinker. Felsham Hall. Gimbert's house. Lovejoy's daughter's private school. This is the Lovejoy world at its glorious best. Even Dandy fares better this week. There are hints about his private life that feel surprisingly progressive for a mid-1980s BBC drama and he even survives an attempted murder after being knocked from his tricycle. Not many supporting characters can boast that particular achievement. We also get Gimbert in a swimming pool. Which leads me to have reached a controversial conclusion after much/some/little consideration. I prefer Gimbert's house to Felsham Hall. Lady Jane's gaff doesn't have a pool. The American contingent arrives in the form of Edward and Nicole, fellow coin hunters who immediately raise suspicions. Nicole's formidable 1980s blonde perm, meanwhile, reduces Lovejoy from respected antiques dealer to warm modelling clay in roughly three seconds. Putty, if you will. The Roman coin hunt itself is good tea time viewing fun. Lovejoy's daughter becomes his Roman tutor, which reminds us that beneath the scams, blagging and occasional dishonesty, Lovejoy is actually a decent father when he remembers he has a daughter. The clues eventually lead to the Isle of Man, where Bexton's posthumous treasure hunt continues. The island itself looks magnificent. The B&B less so. Even the accommodation fails to lift my spirits, despite apparently being good enough for Bexton. Fortunately the plot keeps moving. With help from the landlady, Lovejoy gets steadily warmer in his game of historical Hot and Cold. He seems to get on rather better with this landlady than he does with his own landlord, although admittedly Gimbert has tried to shoot him. Jane and Eric also arrive on the island for reasons best known to themselves and the BBC travel budget. Still, it's nice to have the gang back together. The climax sees Lovejoy abseiling down to inspect the hidden hoard while the remarkably lazy Edward simply hangs around above threatening to take pot-shots at him. Which, by my reckoning, makes it twice in one episode that Lovejoy has been shot at — by two entirely different people. Gimbert with the shotgun in the opening minutes, Edward with the rifle in the closing ones. Quite an achievement, even for our hero. Then comes the twist. Nicole kills Edward. Not brother and sister after all. The final showdown takes place at a dilapidated watermill. Apart from the waterwheel itself, which looks as though someone painted it bright red with Hammerite approximately forty-eight hours before filming started. Nicole turns on Lovejoy one final time but by now the putty has finally hardened and our hero manages to overpower her. We finish appropriately back at Felsham Hall. Jane asks whether Lovejoy kept any of the coins for himself. To his credit he immediately admits he did. "For a rainy day." Moments later Jane somehow ends up apologising to him. What a divvy. A cracking episode. Treasure hunt, Roman coins, attempted murder, double-crosses, Gimbert firing a shotgun at his tenant and Lovejoy once again proving that an attractive blonde can bring his wood to life. The Isle of Man detour works, Bexton's posthumous prank is great fun and the whole thing rattles along like a Volvo estate with questionable brakes. Bexton may be dead, but he's still the cleverest man in the episode. And as for Lovejoy? He's still putty when he sees a bit of skirt or an antique. So am I when I see a Lovejoy episode this good.

title: The Judas Pair
summary: Lovejoy goes hunting for a mythical pair of duelling pistols and somehow ends up trapped in a burning cottage with Jane, a crossbow-wielding maniac and the most dangerous screwdriver in East Anglia.
divvyMoment: La Grange! What a splendid name for a villain
body: One Wink Plot A collector is murdered for a legendary pair of Durs Egg duelling pistols known as The Judas Pair. Unfortunately for the killer, the set is incomplete and Lovejoy knows where the missing turnscrew is. What follows is part detective story, part treasure hunt and part siege movie, proving once and for all that no antique accessory should ever be underestimated. Review "I should have seen the trouble coming." Okay, halfway through Series 1 and this is the big one. Much as The Sopranos has "Whitecaps" and Breaking Bad has "Ozymandias", Lovejoy fans tend to point towards The Judas Pair. If Episode 1 was the proof of concept, this is where the series becomes a legend. As luck would have it, this is one of the few Lovejoy books I've actually read. Years ago I picked up Lovejoy at Large Again, an omnibus containing the first three novels: 1. The Judas Pair 2. Gold From Gemini 3. The Grail Tree In a happy accident, the television series has already adapted the first two in almost exactly the same order. Gold From Gemini became last week's Friends, Romans and Enemies and now we arrive at the original Lovejoy story itself. We begin in a barn where Lovejoy and Michael Seymour are about to duel with a pair of flintlock pistols. At the last moment they deliberately fire away from one another. This is known as deloping and the episode never bothers to explain it, so I'm correcting a forty-year-old oversight on its behalf. Spoiler alert: Michael isn't the villain. More importantly, Michael looks exactly like the villain. Having seen Season 2 , I remain convinced Lovejoy should have shot him. Smug git. The duel exists mainly to explain the central mystery. A man has been murdered and a pair of rare flintlock duelling pistols stolen. Lovejoy is hired to trace them. Off to Cambridge we go. Jane and Lovejoy go punting on the Cam while discussing the mythical thirteenth pair of Durs Egg pistols known as The Judas Pair. The pistols themselves are real enough. Durs Egg was one of London's greatest gunmakers and surviving examples now sell for eye-watering sums. A bit like pints of IPA in London in 2026. Cambridge looks absolutely gorgeous. The colleges, the river, the bridges. The only improvement would have been Eric doing the punting or everyone abandoning the plot entirely and racing around King's College in a low-budget version of Chariots of Fire. Michael wants the Judas Pair as well, although he dismisses them as being about as likely to exist as Excalibur. This, of course, guarantees that Lovejoy will find them. One thing I noticed this time around is that Lovejoy has started wearing the leather jacket. You know the one. Not quite three-quarter length, not quite waist length, permanently attached to Ian McShane for the next several years. No Dandy Jack this week, mind. Last seen face-down beside his tricycle in Friends, Romans and Enemies , he is presumably still convalescing. Given the body count this episode, sensibly so. The investigation takes us to Norfolk where Jane memorably declares: "La Grange! What a splendid name for a villain." The plot is complicated enough that the episode helpfully has Lovejoy drive around in Jane's green Range Rover listing all the suspects like he's hosting East Anglia's answer to Columbo. Then Lovejoy becomes obsessed with a screwdriver. Not the pistols. A screwdriver. A Durs turnscrew, apparently. It looks like something you'd buy from Screwfix for £4.99. Nonetheless Lovejoy becomes so excited by it that he breaks into an auction house in the middle of the day to retrieve it. Jane is getaway driver in her Landrover. Why not. This proves to be a remarkably good instinct because before long people are willing to rob houses, assault Jane and commit arson in pursuit of what is essentially the world's most valuable toolkit accessory. "I have never pretended to understand your friendship with Lovejoy," says Lord Felsham. That makes two of us and possibly the scriptwriters as well. The middle section of this episode is superb. The mystery tightens, the suspects narrow and Lovejoy realises the killer already possesses the Judas Pair but needs the missing turnscrew to complete the set. Suddenly Lovejoy has bait. Watching this episode again, every location is sumptuous. Cambridge. The market squares. Country lanes. Lovejoy's cottage. I worked on Faversham market around the late 80s before school and these scenes press every nostalgia button available. The England of Lovejoy may never have existed exactly as remembered, but it certainly feels like it did. The bucolic dream is eventually interrupted by a crossbow attack, pistol fire and an act of arson that turns Jane's renovation project into a very expensive bonfire. Lovejoy and Jane survive by hiding in the priest hole beneath the cottage, conveniently located next to the booze. Eventually Lovejoy realises the culprit is Dr La Grange and heads off for a final confrontation. And what a confrontation. La Grange doesn't simply confess. He challenges Lovejoy to a duel. I'm still not entirely sure why Lovejoy agrees to this. The turnscrew is returned. The pistols are loaded. And then comes one of the great twists of the entire series. The Judas Pair are called the Judas Pair because one of the pistols is a traitor. Instead of firing forwards, it fires backwards. The duellist pulls the trigger and blows his own brains out. Finally we discover the inscription hidden on the pistols: Rex Me Fecit. "The King made me." Lovejoy realises that some royal figure forced Durs Egg to create the weapons and left a clue hidden in plain sight for future generations. The mystery is solved. And if Rex Me Fecit means "The King made me", then perhaps (maybe gilding the lily slightly here) then Lovejoy Me Fecit. Perfection.

title: To Sleep No More
summary: A cracking opening, a gloriously daft vicar disguise... and a central mystery that never quite wakes up.
divvyMoment: If even half the rumours in this game were true, we'd all be rich
body: One Wink Plot A dead copyist leaves behind a fake snuff box, a fake priest and a real fortune. Unfortunately the middle of the episode gets buried with him. Review Following the near perfection of The Judas Pair was never going to be easy, and To Sleep No More becomes the first episode of Lovejoy that feels a tad ordinary. That's not to say it's bad — Lovejoy is never terrible — but it is the first time Series One has some serious dips. Ironically, it gets almost everything right at the start of the episode. Lovejoy and Eric buzz through the cricket ground gates on the motorcycle/sidecar combo before Charlie Gimbert delivers one of his finest moments. A man collapses and dies in the middle of a village cricket match (the match isn't suspended until the man literally keels over) and Charlie's overwhelming concern isn't grief or sympathy. It's annoyance that his half-century has been denied. Classic Gimbert. The sneer is lovely. The opening continues with the introduction of Arnold Nelson, sporting a moustache now very fashionable in Hoxton and demanding compensation for the "vintage Spode" plates Lovejoy sold him. John Forgeham threatens to blow the bloody doors off the main plot every time Arnold stomps back into the episode — which is rather fitting, given Forgeham also appeared in The Italian Job. The resulting pub fight is magnificent and choreographed with all the swagger of a 1950s Hollywood western. Dandy Jack quietly lends a hand once again and, having previously likened him to Jar Jar Binks, I may owe the man a small apology. He's still not exactly fully formed or certain what he is doing in each episode but he does add something. Unfortunately, once Sam Wendell's funeral begins, the episode loses much of its momentum. The wake (why are the Felshams there!), the lengthy discussions about copyists, forgers and snuff boxes, and the slow drip-feed of clues never quite generate the urgency the opening promises. The central mystery simply isn't as engaging as the colourful cast circling around it. Thankfully Ian McShane drags proceedings back to life once Lovejoy realises a fake priest is hunting the box. Watching him bluff his way around in a dog collar is exactly the sort of stuff I'm here for. The hotel receptionist, meanwhile, somehow identifies Lovejoy as Anglican while Smiley O'Reilly is Roman Catholic after little more than a glance. Personally, I'd quite like five minutes with her myself. I still struggle to explain the difference between Baptists and Methodists, yet she can identify denominations faster than Tinker can knock back a G&T. The episode also expands Lovejoy's growing catalogue of antique folklore. We learn that a "Foreigner" is the extra copy a forger secretly makes for himself, while "Sleepers" are valuable antiques deliberately hidden away until the world forgets they exist. Lovejoy explains these wonderfully romantic concepts to the audience with complete confidence, although apparently not to Eric, who after six episodes still seems to be paying for an apprenticeship without receiving much actual tuition. The script also delivers one of the series' best observations: "If even half the rumours in this game were true, we'd all be rich." It's a lovely line because it captures the entire world of Lovejoy, where whispered legends often prove more valuable than the antiques themselves. Ironically, that's also the episode's biggest weakness. The subplot involving Arnold, Charlie, Smiley O'Reilly and Lovejoy's ecclesiastical adventures is consistently more entertaining than the treasure hunt at the story's heart. When your supporting cast are repeatedly blowing the bloody doors off the central mystery, you know you've got a structural problem. It's an issue the series flirts with again in the following episode, The Real Thing . There's still plenty to enjoy here. McShane remains effortlessly charismatic, Smiley's transformation from petty crook to gun-toting antique hunter is almost as memorable as the Elvis Warhol print hanging on Cecilia Mattock's wall, and the final reveal is satisfyingly neat. But for the first time in Series One, the journey simply isn't as enjoyable as the destination. Favourite Moment Lovejoy borrowing a dog collar and hoping nobody asks too many theological questions. Antique Lesson A Foreigner is the secret extra copy a forger keeps for himself. A Sleeper is an antique deliberately hidden away until the world forgets it exists. The Divvy Verdict An excellent opening, a superb pub fight and Ian McShane having enormous fun pretending to be a vicar can't quite disguise the fact that the middle of the episode is a slog. Still enjoyable, but comfortably the weakest outing of Series One so far.

title: The Real Thing
summary: Two cracking stories compete for centre stage in an overstuffed but thoroughly enjoyable return to form.
divvyMoment: You don't know the difference between a Fabergé and a French fry
body: One Wink Plot Lovejoy flees to Norwich to escape an angry builder, only to uncover a fake painting, a fake antiques empire and a fake businessman. Thankfully, he's the real thing. Review There's something rather fitting about watching The Real Thing during a World Cup. As I write this, Brazil are taking on Japan in the 2026 tournament. Forty years earlier, when this episode first aired, football fans were counting down to Mexico '86 and Diego Maradona's Hand of God. Meanwhile, in East Anglia, Lovejoy was stealing spiral staircases, annoying Charlie Gimbert and exposing counterfeit antiques. History has room for both. After the rather pedestrian To Sleep No More , this is exactly the sort of bounce-back Series One needed. Better still, it ventures beyond Lovejoy's familiar Suffolk stomping grounds and heads north. Well... Norwich. Which introduces us to Lovejoy's answer to the King of the North: Tony Palmer. The opening is superb. Lady Jane is still waiting for the wrought-iron spiral staircase Lovejoy promised her, prompting one of their sweetest exchanges to date. Lovejoy solves the problem in the only way he knows how: by relieving Charlie Gimbert of the very staircase he'd already bought. Strapped to the roof of the Volvo, it looks barely tall enough to reach a windowsill in a bungalow. It also gives Lovejoy two perfectly good reasons to disappear to Norwich. Firstly, there's yet another irate builder threatening to flatten him. Secondly, Lady Jane just happens to have a place to stay while helping furnish Tony Palmer's ambitious new antiques market. A paid job, free accommodation and several counties between yourself and an angry customer? Even Lovejoy couldn't argue with that. The biggest criticism of The Real Thing is also one of its greatest strengths. It contains two genuinely good episodes that have been squeezed into one. The first follows a wonderfully simple painting scam. A retired army officer and his accomplice persuade a kindly shopkeeper that he has stumbled across a priceless George Vincent. The poor fellow — who looks like cricket's Bumble — is only conned because he thinks he's about to con the owner himself. It's a beautifully observed confidence trick and, whisper it quietly, probably a stronger story than anything we got in last week's To Sleep No More . Running alongside it is Tony Palmer's glamorous vision for a new Norwich antiques market. I rather like Tony. He's charming, enthusiastic and possesses the effortless confidence of someone who's never once doubted a word coming out of his own mouth. He doesn't initially feel like a villain at all. In many ways he's Lovejoy's mirror image: another charismatic rogue with a gift for selling dreams. Lovejoy, however, is suspicious from the outset. Not because of any evidence, but because the whole thing simply doesn't feel right. It's the same instinct that tells him when a painting is fake. Palmer has the rented Rolls-Royce, the expensive lunches, the glossy brochures and the salesman's patter, but Lovejoy can sense he isn't the real thing. Mind you, Palmer also commits the cardinal sin of expecting Lovejoy to hold down something resembling a proper job. Watching Lovejoy recoil at business plans, dealer recruitment and salaried employment is reassuring to this slacker. You just know he'd last about three days in a nine-to-five. I rather admire that, having spent thirty years doing jobs that interested me about as much as Tony's interest in Art Deco. Early on, Lovejoy buys twenty cigarettes and a box of matches for the princely sum of £1.41. A few scenes later Tony offers him £250 a week to work for him. By my entirely unqualified Benson & Hedges inflation calculator, that's roughly £3,500 a week in 2026 money. Norwich itself looks magnificent. I've never been, but after watching Lovejoy cruise around in that glorious red Roller, I rather feel I should. The change of scenery freshens everything up after six weeks of the same villages, pubs and auction rooms. The comic centrepiece is undoubtedly Antiques Treasure Trail, the BBC's paper-thin disguise for Antiques Roadshow. I'm still not entirely convinced why Charlie Gimbert suddenly qualifies as an antiques expert, or why the BBC invented a fake version of one of its own programmes, but watching Charlie gradually unravel on camera while Lovejoy quietly rigs proceedings is enjoyable fluff. Pleasingly, Lovejoy never abandons one mystery for the other. While exposing Palmer's fake empire, he also finds time to orchestrate an elaborate counter-con to recover the shopkeeper's money. The mechanics are almost too complicated to summarise, but they bring Tinker and Eric back into the fold and remind us that Lovejoy is always at its best when the whole gang are involved. Poor Dandy Jack, however, continues to drift through Series One like a man who wandered onto the wrong set. Geoffrey Bateman is always good value, but here Dandy appears for little more than two minutes, confirms that the George Vincent is fake and quietly disappears again. After briefly defending him over the last couple of episodes, I'm afraid this outing vindicates my original comparison. Dandy Jack increasingly feels like Lovejoy's Jar Jar Binks — never actively annoying, but a character the writers seem quietly unsure what to do with. A shame, because Bateman deserved more than becoming East Anglia's most overqualified fact-checker. By the end, Tony Palmer's charm finally curdles. The one-year lease, the rented Rolls-Royce, the fake confidence and poor Pierre from Lebanon all reveal a man who wasn't building an antiques market at all — he was building an illusion. The title suddenly makes perfect sense. Almost nothing in the episode is "the real thing". Not the George Vincent. Not Palmer's business. Not the lease. Even the Dufy is copied. The only thing that's consistently genuine is Lovejoy's love of the game. Yep, the episode is overstuffed. Either storyline could comfortably have carried an hour on its own. But unlike To Sleep No More , which suffered because its central mystery couldn't sustain the running time, The Real Thing has the opposite problem. It simply has too many good ideas. That's a much nicer complaint to have. Favourite Moment Charlie Gimbert being spectacularly stitched up on Antiques Treasure Trail. Petty, childish and utterly deserved. Good Quote "You don't know the difference between a Fabergé and a French fry." One of Lovejoy's sharpest put-downs, and a line that probably tells us everything we need to know about Tony Palmer's antiques expertise. Guest Focus — Geoffrey Bateman Geoffrey Bateman once again appears as Dandy Jack, forever one of British television's most familiar faces. Many viewers will remember him as James Hooper ("Hooperman") in This Life, but here he's given precious little to do beyond confirming a fake painting is, well... fake. Dandy Jack has gradually won me over during the first series, but this feels like another reminder that the writers never quite knew how to use him. The Divvy Verdict A busy, witty and thoroughly entertaining return to form. Norwich provides a welcome change of scenery, Tony Palmer is a charismatic foil for Lovejoy, and both the painting con and fake antiques market are entertaining enough to have starred in episodes of their own. Four stars, but only because it tries to squeeze two very good episodes into one.

title: The March of Time
summary: Lovejoy discovers that sometimes the most valuable thing hidden inside an antique isn't gold or jewels, but 170-year-old love letters... and an excuse to impersonate a British Army officer.
divvyMoment: I not only hear you, Lovejoy, I can see both of you
body: One Wink Plot Lovejoy buys an empty French clock, only to discover it contains a cache of love letters written on the eve of the Battle of Waterloo. Naturally this leads to cocaine, forged correspondence, a regimental museum, an auction sting and Ian McShane pretending to be Captain Lovejoy of the Imperial War Museum. Just another week in East Anglia. Review This week's review has been written — or "crafted", as Eric would generously insist — from the New Forest. I've spent the past week enjoying breathtaking scenery, dodging wild horses and, if I'm being completely honest, watching far more World Cup football than any responsible adult should in various Hampshire pubs. It has been a good week. England scraped through, just about, and it turns out my dog Tilly is remarkably relaxed around horses. Which is slightly ironic, because while I've spent the week away from home, The March of Time does exactly the opposite. Lovejoy stays firmly rooted in Suffolk, and after a few Series One excursions that wandered rather too far afield, that's exactly where the series belongs. One of my recurring complaints during Series One has been that the further Lovejoy wanders from Constable Country, the less it actually feels like Lovejoy. Lovejoy out of Suffolk is a reproduction Hay Wain. Fortunately, The March of Time remembers exactly where it should be. There are no international gangsters, no secret organisations and no improbable action sequences. Just an antique dealer, an old clock and a story hidden inside it. In many ways, this feels like the simplest Lovejoy episode so far. After some authentic (?!) haggling with fellow dealer Ricky Price, Lovejoy leaves with two clocks. One becomes a gift for Lady Jane after a charming explanation of why Parliament clocks earned their nickname. The other is little more than an empty shell — Japanese innards are apparently easy to get — destined to receive a modern movement before being sold to "the right punter". Classic Lovejoy. Thankfully, the empty clock turns out to be anything but. Hidden inside are preserved love letters between a young woman named Emma Fairfax and Ensign Richard Parker, written, we are told, in the months leading up to the Battle of Waterloo. It's a sweet premise because, unlike several earlier episodes, the antiques aren't simply window dressing. Remove the clock and the entire story collapses. Without it, the episode would be able to fit on TikTok. This is exactly the sort of plot Lovejoy should be telling. The antique isn't valuable because it's old; it's valuable because of the history concealed within it. The early scenes are strong. The quick chat with Ricky Price is Guy Ritchie-esque — maybe Lovejoy is responsible for Guy Ritchie — the Parliament clock explanation suggests Eric may be getting his money's worth off-screen after all, and Tinker immediately springs into life the moment he hears the letters date from the early nineteenth century. Dudley Sutton is on fine form here. When Lovejoy asks, "Can you hear me?", Tinker's deadpan reply from his bar stool is: "I not only hear you, Lovejoy, I can see both of you." Alcoholism as comedy. Now That's What I Call the 80s. Eric also enjoys one of his better outings. His complaint that they should be "back home trying to make a dishonest living" perfectly sums up his role in the partnership, while his ongoing conversations about heavy metal and not knowing who Leonard Cohen is feel nicely rooted in mid-80s Britain. The episode's guest star is Lysette Anthony as Sophy Fairfax. If you grew up male (or any gender really) in Britain during the 1980s, she probably doesn't need an introduction. She seemed to appear in everything for a while, so it's no major surprise that Lovejoy is instantly smitten. The romance is perhaps the episode's only slightly awkward note through modern eyes. Sergeant Drabble describes the suspect as "five foot nine and in his late thirties" — a witness statement that generously adds a couple of inches and knocks a few years off Ian McShane — but even then the age difference is noticeable. The script performs one final con by suggesting Lovejoy isn't really in love with Sophy at all, but with Emma Fairfax, whose tragic story Sophy has come to embody. Meanwhile, Sophy's brother Michael proves that some mysteries don't require the divvy. Lovejoy concludes confidently that Michael has developed an expensive relationship with Colombian marching powder, although "deduces" feels rather generous. The poor chap spends so much time theatrically sniffing he could track bacon through the New Forest, while his frantic arm movements become so theatrical you half expect him to attack the cameraman. If Lovejoy can break the fourth wall, surely this cocaine-deranged man can as well? Even Eric was probably only a scene away from working it out. Sergeant Drabble also deserves an honourable mention for quietly becoming Series One's own The Thin Blue Line. He's never quite the hero, never quite the villain and almost always arrives about ten minutes after Lovejoy has already solved everything. He isn't flashy, but he's becoming one of those dependable supporting characters whose arrival on screen makes Lovejoy's East Anglia feel like home. The final act is classic (think Brazil 1970) Lovejoy. Our hero blags his way into a regimental museum by introducing himself as Captain Lovejoy from the Imperial War Museum — a disguise that somehow fools everyone in the building — before orchestrating an auction (think Bargain Hunt) to raise money for Sophy without forcing her to sell the letters. Best of all, Charlie Gimbert finally receives a taste of his own medicine. After spending the episode delighting in Lovejoy's disappointment, he proudly walks away believing he's secured the valuable letters. He has the forgeries, though, while Lovejoy heroically returns the originals to the Fairfax family. The closing joke about Basildon Bond paper would need a footnote now to explain to younger viewers who think Kindles are old hat. Time really has marched on. And that's what The March of Time understands better than a few earlier episodes. The real treasure isn't money. It's the stories that survive long after the people who wrote them have gone. England may or may not finally bring football home this summer. Lovejoy, meanwhile, has already worked out that the real treasures aren't made of gold. They're the stories that somehow survive the passing years. After all, there's probably an antique dealer somewhere who could tell you the Jules Rimet trophy is a reproduction anyway. Like the empty clock itself, this episode proves that what matters most isn't the mechanism inside, but what time has chosen to preserve.

title: Death in Venice (Parts 1 & 2)
summary: Lovejoy trades Suffolk mud for Venetian canals in the series' only feature-length outing — forged Old Masters, identical twins, dubious Australians and a conspiracy so tangled even Lovejoy has to explain it twice.
body: One Wink Plot The murder of Campie drags Lovejoy from Suffolk to Venice, where a simple question about forged Renaissance paintings unravels into an underground forgery workshop, identical twins, shifty Australians, undercover police officers and a criminal network run by the urbane Pinder. Double-crosses pile onto fake identities until even Lovejoy admits "everything got blurred" — and he should know, because he has to explain the whole conspiracy twice before anyone lets him go home. Fortunately Suffolk, Lucky Luciano and one perfectly timed question from Lady Jane are waiting at the other end. Review "I know, it's pathetic." The World Cup has ended. I'm writing this exactly a week after a great tournament finished with a massively disappointing final. At least the Argies didn't win. Quite aptly, Lovejoy Series One also ends with the massively disappointing Death in Venice, parts one and two. This double-header is an absolute mess — much like the World Cup half-time show. And much as with the original Ronaldo and Ronaldinho appearing in a go-kart with Madonna, I'm not sure even Pelé appearing on a gondola could have saved it. Also like the World Cup, it'll be a few years — five, in this case — until we get another outing. Death in Venice was very nearly the death of Lovejoy. I'm reviewing this as a single episode because a) I don't want to write two reviews for this mess, and b) I don't want the overall Series One score dragged down by two horrible episodes. This story went out in 1986 and was probably filmed in 1985, at a time when there was no James Bond in place. Roger Moore had retired after A View to a Kill — reportedly after realising he was older than the mother of his leading lady, Tanya Roberts — and part of me thinks this was McShane auditioning for the role. We have Pinder in his wheelchair as the Blofeld-style baddie, with a plot to remove all of Venice's artwork that's only marginally less silly than the one in On Her Majesty's Secret Service, where Blofeld sets up a clinic in the Swiss Alps, recruits a dozen young women with various allergies and hypnotises them into carrying bacteriological agents to wipe out the world's crops and livestock. Anyway — I don't think McShane was ever in with a shout for Bond, but part of me would love to have seen him abseiling into Gibraltar as Dalton eventually did in the opening of The Living Daylights. Could have been Lovejoy. McShane pulls in his real-life wife, Gwen Humble, to play two parts as the twins Caterina and Lavinia — and incredibly, this is nowhere near the worst thing about the episode. Once again the story starts in Suffolk, and all is well. Nice shots, a slightly upsetting murder, and we're off. Unfortunately, we're off to Venice. Now, I went to Venice in the early 90s as part of an Inter-Railing break — about seven years after this was filmed — and having never been back, the episode does remind me of what I saw. So you'd think some nostalgia points would be awarded. But no. I'm not sure why we're there, and neither does anyone in the cast seem to be sure. Someone attempts to explain the plot about three or four times. Lovejoy goes into the Venice lagoon twice, just so we're aware he is in Venice and that Venice has water. Part one ends on a cliffhanger with a very odd shooting — reminiscent of the ending of Get Carter (the Michael Caine Geordie original) but without any of the plot leading up to it. Part two is better: Fulton Mackay turns up and saves the episode. His expert-forger schtick works nicely alongside Lovejoy. Mackay passed away before Series Two came around, but I can't help feeling Lucky would have been a brilliant addition to the regular cast — and with the La Frenais link between Lovejoy and Porridge, they could certainly have made it work. Imagine if Norman Stanley Fletcher had made a crossover appearance. That thought makes me happy. Anyway, the story ends with Lovejoy and Lucky bringing the whole sham down by pulling a Venetian wall over with a boat, flooding the forgery centre that was copying Venice's artwork so Pinder could make off with the real stuff. Truly insane. And not insanely entertaining, unfortunately. I think the scriptwriters understood this, because one of the final scenes is back in the pub in Suffolk — and this pub scene looks better than all the Venice scenes combined — with our famous five (Janey, Gimbert, Tinker, Eric and Lovejoy) trying to explain away what has happened over the previous two hours. It still makes no sense. The final exchange with Jane is great, as she openly admits she's jealous at the thought of Lovejoy sleeping with one of the many women he met on his Venetian jaunt. A fantastic bit of dialogue — up there with Han Solo just before he gets carbonited: Lovejoy: Lady Felsham, I do believe you're jealous. Jane: No, I am not! Lovejoy: Yes, you are. Jane: I know, it's pathetic. So, without overdoing the Star Wars comparison, the BBC — like Boba Fett — take Lovejoy away for a few years. We will return, and Series Two is right up there with Return of the Jedi. The series will be unfrozen. We'll have moved into the 90s, and while it may only have been five years, the Britain that Lovejoy returns to feels completely different. Bring. It. On. Guest Focus — Fulton Mackay & Gwen Humble To an entire generation Fulton Mackay will forever be Mr Mackay, the parade-ground prison officer glowering at Ronnie Barker across the landings of Porridge. Here he turns up as the splendidly named Lucky Luciano — no relation, presumably, to the New York mob boss — and proceeds to walk off with every scene he's given. His unexpected reappearance in Suffolk for the final act is one of the two-parter's genuine pleasures. The other notable piece of casting is Gwen Humble, who plays both Caterina and Lavinia — and who happened, at the time, to be Mrs Ian McShane in real life. Playing identical twins opposite your own husband while he romances his way around Venice is a curious day at the office, but she handles the dual role convincingly, which is more than can be said for some of the plot around her. Trivia & Observations - Part One aired on 7 March 1986 and Part Two on 14 March 1986, the week after The March of Time . - It was also the Series One finale — and the last new Lovejoy on British television for nearly five years. The BBC didn't bring the series back until January 1991. - The story draws on Jonathan Gash's 1984 novel The Gondola Scam, while the title tips its hat to Thomas Mann's novella (and Visconti's 1971 film) — lofty company for a show about a Suffolk antiques dealer. - The climactic escape is scored with a jaunty variation on the Lovejoy theme, which rather undercuts any tension the sequence was hoping to build. - The plot becomes so involved that Lovejoy delivers two full explanations of it — once to Cosima after she's shot, and again back in Suffolk for Jane, Eric, Tinker and Gimbert. - Gimbert's end-of-series audit: "Sod all to show for it again."

title: Just Desserts
summary: Lovejoy walks out of an open prison after eight months inside for handling stolen goods, and sets about finding out exactly who put him there.
divvyMoment: Woolworth's used to sell these for thruppence
body: One Wink Plot Lovejoy walks out of an open prison after eight months inside for handling a stolen Georges Jacob dressing table, a conviction he maintains belongs to somebody else entirely. Clearing his name means unpicking the sting that put him there — a Dutch woman who vanished, a table that found its way home via police custody, and an Old Master hidden somewhere it had no business being. Also a cricket pavilion, a chimney, and a very great deal of Suffolk. Review "Woolworth's used to sell these for thruppence. That's about what they're worth now." It is August 2026 and most of England is in the worst drought since... well, a long time ago. I for one am sick of the heat, and so seeing Lovejoy emerge from an open prison into an overcast afternoon and an awaiting Janey — in her green Range Rover — makes me long for autumn and an end to this hot horror. Lovejoy is back after a five-year episode drought, and McShane emerges into the nineties with more mullet and a little extra body timber. I exited the nineties in similar fashion. McShane had starred in Texan soap opera behemoth Dallas in between and — this is some trivia — had married Sue Ellen Ewing as the English screenwriter Don Lockwood. So, a busy man. Where we left Series One with Fulton Mackay and the Porridge link (Clement, La Frenais), we reappear with a great set-up: Lovejoy in prison and with a score to settle. Luckily this episode stays almost entirely in Suffolk. There is a brief flirtation with Antwerp, but then I imagine the controller at the BBC radioed them to call McShane back after the Death in Venice debacle, and reminded the writers where their strength lay. This episode is a corker. It opens with Lovejoy holding court to a group of Women's Institute members in a hall that resembles one found in any market town. In this cut-price Antiques Roadshow setting we get an antique condom joke, and to my mind, after five years away, that is quite a ballsy opening if you will. The crew are back. Mainly. We seem to have lost Gimbert, but Jane, Eric, Tinker and Lovejoy are all back and looking great. We also get introduced to a new character — Miriam the Morris Minor, a gift from Lady Jane — who will stay with us until the last episode. Shame about the Volvo estate, but this is the nineties and that is progress, I suppose. Onto the plot. A Dutch woman with excellent manners and an antiques shop that turns out not to exist pays Lovejoy £500 to run a Georges Jacob dressing table over to a dealer on the Continent, where it sells for £57,000 and she promptly stops existing as well. The table then contrives to get itself burgled back to its original owner, which is exactly the sort of thing furniture does when there is a stolen Van Dyck folded up inside it. Eric appears in a Lazer crash helmet (still with motorcycle and sidecar). I know of these as they were the cheapest crash helmets you could get in the early nineties, and I had one to accompany the Yamaha DT50 that was my pride and joy when I turned 16. Fifty ccs of pure trail bike power. Nought to thirty in about a minute. Sixth form let me ride it in. At 17 I moved up to an RD125 — liquid cooled, no less. That got stolen, but I had fallen off it about ten times by then so probably for the best. The Lazer crash helmet survived. Anyway. Michael. It was obvious from the wonderful Series One episode The Judas Pair that this friend of the Felshams was a wrong 'un, so when he turns up here — a nice bit of continuity and a great call-back to the highlight of Series One — it is no real surprise that the whole set-up of Lovejoy over the dressing table was led by this bloke. The flashbacks to the sting that got Lovejoy incarcerated are well executed: a brief interlude, fading in and out of black and white. I wish the live cricket on Sky would do the same. I have lost count of the number of times I have celebrated a wicket in the pub only to realise they are showing a previously taken one. Sky, take note — do your replays in black and white so we can differentiate between them and the live action. Talking of cricket, we do get a little cricket in this episode, and a truly strange scene where Lovejoy's fellow ex-con Mavis (a bloke) is tied up in a cricket changing room, about to be tortured by one of Michael's accomplices. Mavis is saved by Lovejoy, who throws cricket balls at the torturer and then drinks cans of Fosters with him — which in my book feels like an unnecessary continuation of the torture. The episode keeps up a nice pace as Lovejoy zones in on his hapless quarry. The first visit to Michael's gaff, where it is Lovejoy professing his innocence, is well handled, and the not-so-subtle interloping of some cockney chimney sweeps leads us to the comedy moment where Lovejoy breaks into the house Santa Claus style to prove who set him up. The final denouement of Michael is a little anti-climactic, but shows up Lovejoy as the bigger man. So the drought is over, and this episode is a welcome shower of Lovejoy... joy, to get us going again. Lovejoy has his cottage back, the gang are back, and I am back. Let's go. Favourite Moment Lovejoy rescuing Mavis from the cricket pavilion by bowling at his torturer, then settling down with him afterwards over warm cans of Fosters. A rescue and a second, subtler cruelty in the same scene. Good Quote Lovejoy, signing off from the Women's Institute: "I have enjoyed these quiet afternoons. Surrounded by nice people talking about their hydrangeas and swapping chutney recipes. Makes a welcome change from the conniving, backstabbing, avaricious alcoholics that populate the antique trade." Guest Focus — Anthony Valentine Anthony Valentine returns as Michael Seymour — the same character, five years and one series on. In The Judas Pair he stood in a barn and deliberately fired wide rather than shoot Lovejoy, and turned out not to be the villain. Here he is the villain, and the eight months Lovejoy has just served are his doing. The payoff to a set-up nobody knew was a set-up in February 1986. Also worth a mention: Christine Kavanagh as Renata Van Der Zee and Maxine Audley as Marigold Paynter. The Divvy Verdict A great return, and good to see Michael get his comeuppance at last — even if Lovejoy lets him off rather more lightly than I would have.

title: The Italian Venus
summary: Lady Jane drags Lovejoy to drinks with the appalling Carey-Holdens, where a catalogue from the Grand Tour turns up a Florentine bronze worth two million — and the disinherited younger brother turns out to have exactly the skills required to relieve the elder one of a fifth of it.
divvyMoment: Your foul little plan appears to be working
body: One Wink Plot Lady Jane cashes in a favour and drags Lovejoy to drinks with Sir Hugo and Lady Felicity Carey-Holden, to price up whatever their great-great-grandfather shipped home from the Grand Tour. Almost all of it is junk. The exception, buried in the catalogue as School of Florence, is a Nicolo Gorini bronze worth two million — and Lovejoy works out where it went long before its owners do. Since Hugo has also cheerfully disinherited his younger brother Douglas, who paints and casts bronze rather too well, that knowledge soon finds a use. Review "And I discovered that Lovejoy is a banger." — Count Binface, candidate for Clacton It is still August and it is still a drought. The grass has gone the colour of a manila envelope and the water company has started using the word "resilience" in its letters, which is what companies write when they mean "no". It is also the week of the Clacton by-election, a contest Nigel Farage arranged for himself by resigning the seat he won two years ago, on the grounds that the voters of Clacton — rather than, say, the Parliamentary Standards Commissioner — should be the ones to judge the £5 million a crypto investor handed him in April 2024. He has explained that the money was for his personal security. He has also explained that it was a reward for twenty-seven years of campaigning for Brexit. He appears genuinely baffled that anyone might look at either explanation, or at both of them standing next to each other, and wonder whether a gift that size ever really arrives without strings. Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Greens and Restore Britain have all declined to turn up at all. That leaves a record thirty-four candidates on the ballot and exactly one real challenger: an intergalactic warrior in a wheelie bin, whose manifesto commits him to justice, lasers, affordable croissants and the return of Ceefax. Asked what he had found on this planet worth the trouble of defending, he gave the answer at the top of this page. So this week, for once, the bridge built itself. Binface will not win. But he has already made his opponent look like a bad Mussolini reproduction: heavy on the jaw, light on the provenance. Which, as it happens, is more or less this week's subject. And talking of punchable faces, The Italian Venus has a magnificent one. Sir Hugo Carey-Holden is Patrick Malahide, who by 1991 had spent the best part of a decade as DS Charlie Chisholm in Minder, being outmanoeuvred week after week by a second-hand car dealer and his minder. He is not even half the cast. Celia Imrie plays his wife, decades before the nation came to know her for something rather less refined — of which more below. Nicholas Farrell, who played Aubrey Montague in Chariots of Fire, is his disinherited brother. Ian McNeice is the expert. Quite a crew for a Sunday night in the early nineties. And the episode is a gem. It opens in a saleroom (as the best Lovejoy episodes do), in that peculiar auction dialect of winks, half-nods and eyebrow-bids where a man can spend eight hundred pounds without appearing to move a muscle, and where Lovejoy watches a bronze horse after Landseer go under the hammer while quietly noting three things: that it is a fake, that it is the third one he has seen, and — the line that sets the whole hour running — that it is possibly better than the original. From there he is dragged into helping Lady Jane, which this week means an afternoon with more of her awful friends. That is two weeks running if we count Michael from Just Desserts , and I am starting to think Jane's address book — the Felshams' more generally — is the most dangerous object in Suffolk. Pleasingly, the treasure is another plain thing. Not a jewel, not a canvas, but what looks for all the world like an outsized soap dish: half a Renaissance bronze group, a scallop shell with seahorses on it, which once carried a nude Venus in the manner of Botticelli's The Birth of Venus. It has spent the last few decades in a goldfish pond, being rained on. Lovejoy helps out. Then the helping-out twists, as it always does, and for his trouble he is clouted round the head by the very man he is trying to help. Structurally this is the first proper Lovejoy builds a sting of the nineties run, and it is all the better for being simple: no murder, no chase, just a greedy man being sold exactly what he asked for. Lovejoy goes to hospital — well, is abandoned there — and gets some stitches from a student. Eric: "I've seen better needlework on a Sunday joint." He will be back at this hospital in the farcical Eric of Arabia in Series Three. Which is where the episode properly gets going, because a clout round the head has never once stopped Lovejoy having an idea. The idea needs Gervais Rackham, and the scene where Lovejoy recruits him is the best two minutes in the hour. Rackham asks, reasonably, whether he is being blackmailed. "Nearly," says Lovejoy. Ian McNeice plays the whole thing like a man being force-fed an enormous cake entirely against his will, and I could watch him do it all afternoon. All Rackham has to do, he is assured, is identify a genuine Gorini as a genuine Gorini — which is perfectly true, and also the most dishonest sentence in the episode. Then the squeeze. Lovejoy floats the Venus at ninety-five grand and lets it climb to two hundred and twelve for cash — and never once tells Hugo he already owns the other half. He lets Rackham do that by accident, on a stroll round the garden, where the missing shell has been gurgling away in the goldfish pond for decades. Hugo is never actually sold anything. He is simply allowed to work out, all by himself, that he is about to be very clever. Which is when the Carey-Holdens damn themselves. Rackham was promised one per cent for finding the shell — thirty or forty thousand — so having found it, Hugo decides a verbal agreement isn't an agreement and noticing something in a garden isn't finding it. Rackham settles for a thousand. Felicity leans in to ask whether that includes VAT. Anyone who has ever sent an invoice will feel a vein go. She then trims Lovejoy's fee too, and tells him kindly that she doesn't blame him for trying it on. These people are being relieved of a fifth of a million pounds and they still cannot stop haggling over the tip. But the thing that makes the episode is the lamp. Lovejoy dreams about the bronze and wakes up knowing. The real Venus — the two-million-pound one, the half everybody has spent the hour hunting — has been standing in the drawing room all along with a shade on its head. Grandpa sawed the group in two: the shell went in the pond, the goddess got wired for electricity. So Jane takes Felicity out to lunch, and Lovejoy sells a rich man a forgery in a room containing the original. The wash-up is genuinely warm, which not every Lovejoy sting manages. Douglas gets his inheritance in cash — not all of it, but a good deal more than Hugo ever intended him to see. Rackham has been showing the bronze horse round the trade to universal praise, so Douglas ends the hour as a coming man with two agents circling him and ten per cent going to whichever he likes best. Eric requires lager, dry-roasted crisps and pork scratchings. And Jane's mysterious favour, hanging over the whole episode, turns out to be two months' free rent. Then Hugo rings. He now owns two bronzes, one of which he paid a fortune for, and he has a suggestion about where the next one is going. We never hear the end of the sentence, which is the correct decision. Favourite Moment Normally this is where I pick a scene. Not this week. My favourite moment is the discovery that somewhere on Thursday's ballot paper there is a candidate for the United Kingdom Parliament whose manifesto commits him, in writing, to Lovejoy. Not "the arts". Not "our television heritage". Lovejoy — sandwiched between affordable croissants and the return of Ceefax. Thirty-five years after this episode went out on a Sunday night, a man in a wheelie bin has done more for Lovejoy's standing than anyone has managed since the show ended in 1994. I have no idea what he would make of the Gorini, but I am fairly confident he would have spotted the lamp. Good Quote Gervais Rackham, ringing in with a progress report he is enjoying far more than he will admit: "Your foul little plan appears to be working." Guest Focus — Celia Imrie Celia Imrie is Lady Felicity Carey-Holden — four years before Acorn Antiques made her a household fixture, and a full thirty-four before she achieved a rather different sort of immortality by breaking wind on national television in The Celebrity Traitors. There is no career plan that gets you from one of those to the other. She should be extremely proud of both. What she does here is cleverer than simply playing snobbish. Felicity is the one angling for free valuations, the one who says "yah", and the one who personally short-changes both the expert and the con man on her husband's instructions while remaining perfectly, blithely charming about it. She is also the last person on screen, admiring a forgery in her own drawing room and finding it strangely familiar. {/* Notes not used in the prose — kept for reference, delete before commit if you want the file clean: - Tinker is entirely absent. Dudley Sutton is in Just Desserts and back for Bin Diving, but not here. Eric carries the whole sidekick load, a chunk of it spent barking at the door and being told to fetch himself a bone. - Series Two was shot in Oxfordshire as a cost saving before the production returned to Suffolk for Series Three and stayed. NEEDS A SECOND SOURCE before it goes on the site — locations are a known gap. - Continuity wobble: the Grand Tour is Hugo's great-GREAT-grandfather in the catalogue scene, but by the drawing room it is "your great-grandfather", and the man who sawed it up is "Grandpa Carey-Holden". - Douglas's wife is called Anna throughout the dialogue but credited as Emma Holden. - Archie Duncannon, the dead V&A man whose name Lovejoy plants at the auction and cashes in two acts later. - The bank scene: a £212,000 banker's draft cashed indoors while a traffic warden escalates over a yellow line outside. Cut from the prose. - The FTSE bulletin on the television, with the 100 Share Index closing at 2346.2, "its highest since early February". Cut with the bank scene — still the best period detail available if a slot opens up elsewhere. - Lovejoy's lock-picking, learned "in one of Her Majesty's holiday camps". */} The Divvy Verdict Anyway — I like this episode. We don't have any Tinker so it can't be a full five, but this is an episode that ticks all of my Lovejoy boxes and, whilst I was born on planet earth, if I wasn't I would have been happy to spaceship over to watch it.

title: Bin Diving
summary: One elderly widow, one pair of Purdeys and Warren Clarke going through the bins. Lovejoy discovers that in Suffolk even the rubbish is antique.
divvyMoment: We junk half our history every year
body: One Wink Plot One elderly widow, one pair of Purdeys and Warren Clarke going through the bins. Lovejoy discovers that in Suffolk even the rubbish is antique. Review We are, apparently, heading into heatwave number six of 2026. Six. They have stopped feeling like weather events and started feeling like a subscription I do not remember signing up for. The heat has got to me, obviously, because I had the Clacton by-election filed in my head as something that had already happened. It hasn't. It was originally pencilled in for the sixth, Tendring District Council moved it back a week, and somewhere in that shuffle my brain quietly marked it done. It is, in fact, this Thursday. Count Binface remains on the ballot. I remain hopeful. It has been a strange week regardless. Critical systems went down at work, and there is nothing like several hundred people discovering simultaneously that they cannot do their jobs to make a man long for the simplicity of a small antiques emporium in Suffolk. No incident calls, no status page, no war room. Just a shop, a kettle, and somebody's grandmother trying to sell you a toffee hammer. And then the weekend, which I am spending reliving my youth over in nearby Lewisham, watching Grooverider. I have not seen him since I was a mop-haired teenager at Reincarnation at the King's Hall — rave geeks may look that one up at their leisure — and I regret to report that the intervening years have done their work. These days I bear rather more resemblance to something found at the bottom of a refuse sack. Which leads us very nicely into Bin Diving. The last episode had a two-million-pound bronze and a baronet. This one has a rubbish round in the rain, and is much the better hour for it. Nobody leaves Suffolk, and nobody tries to make Lovejoy into anything other than a man who knows what things are worth. The opening has aged wonderfully. Nothing is sorted; it all goes into the same sacks, and the nearest thing Suffolk has to a circular economy is Warren Clarke going through them looking for Georgian silver. "We junk half our history every year," says Lovejoy. "We throw away millions." Recycling in 1991 appears to consist of putting absolutely everything in one bin and hoping the dustman has an eye. He does. Brian Nunn's round carries tottin' rights, meaning first refusal on anything worth having, and Eric, who calls the practice scratching, has been quietly infringing them. The double act that follows needs both halves, and Chris Jury is why it works. For a few scenes you could happily watch a spin-off consisting entirely of the two of them driving round Suffolk going through other people's bins. It is also one of the rare occasions Eric is shown to have a life of his own. The plot arrives with Jane asking Lovejoy to do a favour for a friend, a sentence that should by now land like Columbo stopping in the doorway, apparently satisfied, and turning back to say there is just one small thing still bothering him. Mrs Jaglom needs ten thousand pounds for a leaking roof, her late husband having left his affairs in the usual condition, and her relatives are already helping themselves. Did I mention the rain? The episode is drenched in it, and watching a Suffolk downpour during the worst drought in fifty years is its own small cruelty. Miriam sits out in it looking exactly as an old Morris Minor ought to look in a Lovejoy episode: wet. I have had Creedence Clearwater Revival's Have You Ever Seen the Rain? going round my head all week, which is not helping. Upstairs there is a Gainsborough, or rather there isn't. It is Mary, Countess Howe, whose original hangs at Kenwood, and this one is a Victorian copy worth about £1,500 — fifteen per cent of a roof. Mrs Jaglom takes the news, addresses some remarks to her late husband on the subject of where he now is, and smashes it herself. I cannot remember the last proper attic scene before this one, possibly not since The Firefly Cage . Dandy Jack somehow survives into Series Two, though only at the other end of a telephone. I have a theory about this: that the script was written with a proper part for him, that nobody thought to mention he had been quietly dropped after Series One, and that he was therefore demoted to a landline and left exactly where he was. This is as close to Geoffrey Bateman as we are now going to get, and it may also mark the start of a running count of the landline calls in this programme, which is going to be a large number. Miriam breaks down in a ford that looks a great deal like the water Lovejoy and Eric first drenched Lady Jane in back in The Firefly Cage . Either a quiet callback or a location manager who had found somewhere good and saw no reason to go looking twice. Alexander is away, and Lovejoy ends up on Jane's couch. This becomes inconvenient the following morning, when Mrs Jaglom is attacked and two policemen want to know where he spent the night. He declines to tell them, because telling them would embarrass Jane. Just Lovejoy. Gentleman. The policemen are DS Bentley, down from the Met to instil some rigour, and DC Hubbard. Neil Dudgeon plays Bentley straight and without humour, which is right, and plainly learning his trade two decades before Midsomer Murders handed him a county of his own. "I'm determined to nick you, Lovejoy." "I admire people who are big on principles." Brian, meanwhile, has established where Bentley lives, and raises the possibility of his bins going uncollected. Catching the culprits takes plan B: poster a town, take a room at the Women's Institute, offer free valuations and wait. Three toffee hammers later, in walk two young men with a rhino horn they found on a tip: a pair of floppy-haired Hooray Henrys who, cast today, would be third and fourth Targaryen from the left in House of the Dragon. Lovejoy gives them twenty pounds for it. It has Major Jaglom's name on it. What they were after is a matched pair of Purdeys, bought in 1938 and eventually fetching £30,000. Only a few episodes after The Judas Pair , valuable shotguns are back on the premises. Lovejoy appears to exist in a universe containing about six valuable objects, and sooner or later all of them come round again. Then the ending, which is the best thing in it: the pair of them in the back of the lorry with the rubbish, and Brian working the compactor until a confession arrives. Favourite Moment Brian strolls into the workshop looking for Lovejoy and finds Eric pointing a gun at him instead. "Staffordshire figure or your life, you fat slug." Eric spends most of this programme being sent on errands and told to fetch things, so the sight of him holding up a man twice his size over a bit of Staffordshire is a genuine pleasure. Brian's only complaint afterwards is that Lovejoy really ought to instruct his staff about lines of demarcation. Good Quote "You're extracting a confession under duress, Lovejoy." "Oh, well, do it your way then." Guest Focus — Warren Clarke Warren Clarke arrives fully formed as Brian Nunn and should never have been allowed to leave. Brian is intimidating and funny in the same breath, knows his antiques, runs a small parallel economy out of other people's rubbish, wears a trucker's cap decades before that meant anything, and drives a lorry with horns and bears bolted to the front, like something that has wandered in from Toy Story. He is also, without explanation, a serious cook: found mid-recipe worrying about his cream curdling, and late to the ambush because he needed a coconut. His wife is a midwife and prefers pie and a pint. Nobody remarks on any of it, which is exactly why it works. He never appears again, which is the one genuine complaint available against the episode. The Divvy Verdict Five out of five, with no Tinker in it. I docked The Italian Venus a star for that very absence a fortnight ago. I have no defence and I am not going to construct one. It works because it is Lovejoy operating entirely within its natural habitat: Suffolk, antiques, rain, petty crooks, Jane, Eric, and eccentrics who were clearly there long before anyone thought to film them. The previous episode reached for something bigger. This one goes smaller and is far better for it. And it has the sense to finish on the two Hooray Henrys picking through the rubbish themselves. A couple of bin divers. {/* Verified against the episode script: - Gainsborough copy of Mary, Countess Howe, valued at "about £1,500" against the £10,000 Mrs Jaglom needs. Mat's 15% was exactly right. - Purdeys bought by Major Jaglom in 1938 (Lovejoy phones Purdey's, whose records go back to the last century); Lot 200 sells at £30,000. - Bentley's line is "I admire people who are big on principles", not "I'm big on people with principles" as the Lovejoy Antiques Wiki has it. Still unverified, so left out: - "First attic scene since The Firefly Cage" — phrased as a recollection. The script never names the room, and the reviews do not catalogue every scene, so it is not provable either way. - The landscape said to resemble the fjord/river location from Series One. Locations remain a known gap and nothing sources it. Cut for length, still available: - Eric sells Lovejoy's Charles II walnut chair to Betty Morgan of Betty's Bygones for £1,000 to raise the cash for the Purdeys. It goes for £2,900 at the same auction that sells the guns, so Eric was robbed and the episode never says so. - Brian on bin diving: persistent offenders end up in the fracture clinic. - The tip scene: Lovejoy wading through the rubbish while Brian supervises from dry ground, warning him off the cat litter and insisting the smell is perfume, the place being a bed of roses. Was the Favourite Moment before the Eric hold-up took the slot. - Lovejoy to Brian, on the sacks tipped over him: "Do I give a discount for dust?" - Writer Terry Hodgkinson, director Baz Taylor. */}
